prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We could hear her knocking down strands of cobweb from ceilings—sticky filaments, sacs of eggs—as we woke most mornings to a worm of discontent. It lodged beneath the heart, rubbed our frayed nerves, gnawed at the gut, spleen, ovaries. Filth was Mom's first enemy, so each day began with ritual cleaning: the stab and sweep of the broom down the dark hall, over the stained and scratched oak floors. For weeks, she held her dust mop one-handed, and with the other cupped a hernia, while she swore at us kids in that hard voice—a litany of our sins and failures: sloth, stupidity, secrecy. We watched her smash the spiders that ran, herky-jerky, along the baseboards, while we ran, too. Glaring at each other, we gathered up the scattered laundry, our father’s shoes, his newspapers and tools, our books, drawings, music, sweatshirts, and jackets, whatever we’d left lying around. We were guilty, but good at evasion. We cultivated shrewish or obsessive behaviors of our own: my tough older sister sneered and stalked out of the house to meet her boyfriend; my sweet younger sister trembled and cried, comforted by one of our many dogs. I slammed doors, pounded them with my fists, screamed, “Shut up, shut up, shut up!” She couldn’t leave us alone. She loved us too much. Though we were quick, she was quicker. Her words stung. We must have deserved it.

Keywords: Filth, Mom, For

outputs.L2: Most mornings, as we were waking into a small, wormlike misery, we could hear her clearing the ceilings of cobwebs—tacky threads and egg sacs coming down. The feeling settled under the heart, scraped against our raw nerves, and chewed at the stomach, the spleen, the ovaries. Dirt was Mom’s chief adversary, so every day opened with a kind of cleaning ceremony: the broom jabbing and swishing through the dim hallway and across the scarred, stained oak floors. For several weeks she gripped the dust mop in one hand and held a hernia with the other, all while cursing us children in her harsh voice, reciting our offenses and defects—laziness, foolishness, dishonesty. We saw her crush the spiders that skittered in jerky bursts along the baseboards, and we fled as well. Shooting angry looks at one another, we picked up the mess: loose laundry, Dad’s shoes, his papers and tools, our books, sketches, music, sweatshirts, jackets—anything we had abandoned. We were at fault, but we knew how to dodge blame. Each of us developed our own sharp or compulsive habits: my hard-edged older sister would sneer and stride out to see her boyfriend; my gentle younger sister would shake and sob, soothed by one of our many dogs. I banged doors, beat on them with my fists, and yelled, “Shut up, shut up, shut up!” Mom could not simply let us be. She cared about us too intensely. We were fast, but she was faster. Her language hurt. We must have had it coming.
outputs.L3:
The narrator’s mother began each day with a fierce and almost ritual commitment to cleaning. For her, dirt and disorder were not ordinary inconveniences but enemies to be defeated before anything else could happen. Filth was, in her mind, the first threat of the day, and she met it with relentless energy and determination.

This daily battle continued even when her body was in pain. She cleaned as if she had no choice, pushing herself beyond comfort or reason. At times, she would hold a hernia in place with one hand while sweeping with the other, all the while scolding her children for the disorder around her. Her physical suffering did not soften her anger; instead, it seemed to sharpen it, making the household atmosphere even more tense.

The children were often blamed for the mess, for the scattered belongings, and even for the family’s larger failures and frustrations. Under their mother’s angry gaze, they learned to move quickly, trying to gather up whatever had been left lying around before it could provoke another outburst. Their efforts were not only attempts to clean but also attempts to protect themselves from her disappointment and rage.

Each child responded differently to life in this strained household. Some became defiant, resisting their mother’s authority in whatever ways they could. Others cried, overwhelmed by the pressure and accusation. Some tried to avoid her altogether, disappearing from the scene before they could be blamed. Still others absorbed the tension and turned it into rage of their own. The home was shaped by these different responses, all of them born from the same atmosphere of fear, guilt, and emotional intensity.

Yet the narrator does not present the mother’s harshness as simple cruelty. Her anger, discipline, and exhausting demands are shown as inseparable from an overwhelming love. She fought dirt, disorder, and failure because she believed she was protecting her family from shame and collapse. For the children, this made their feelings even more complicated. They feared her and resented her, but they also understood that her severity came from devotion. As a result, their memories of her are marked not only by pain, but also by guilt: guilt for failing to meet her expectations, guilt for resenting her, and guilt for being loved so fiercely by someone whose love could feel like punishment.
outputs.L4:
Every morning in our house began with the sound of my mother cleaning.

Before anyone had spoken, before the kettle had boiled, before the children had fully remembered who they were and what trouble they might already be in, there was the scrape of a chair being dragged across the floor, the slap of a wet cloth against the kitchen table, the sharp clatter of dishes being rearranged in cupboards where they had already been arranged the night before. My mother moved through the rooms with the urgency of someone trying to stop a disaster from happening, though the disaster was never named. It lived in dust on the mantelpiece, fingerprints on the glass, a spoon left in the sink, a sock curled beneath the radiator like a dead mouse.

She saw everything. A cobweb trembling in the corner above the back door could darken her whole face. Crumbs beneath the table were proof of carelessness, laziness, disrespect. A schoolbag abandoned in the hallway became evidence in a trial that had begun long before breakfast. We learned to read the house the way others might read the weather. If the mop bucket was out, we kept quiet. If she was wiping the same clean counter again and again, we avoided her eyes. If she began opening drawers, searching for disorder, then one of us would find a reason to disappear upstairs, into the bathroom, out to the bins, anywhere we might be temporarily beyond reach.

But there was no real hiding from her. Her voice could travel through walls.

“Who left this here?”

No one answered at first. We looked at one another, each hoping the guilty person would confess, each afraid that silence would make us all guilty together. Sometimes it was mine. Sometimes it was my brother’s, or my sister’s. Sometimes it belonged to no one in particular: a cup, a coat, a smear of toothpaste in the sink. In our house, objects seemed to betray us. They appeared where they should not be and carried our names in secret.

My mother’s anger was not wild at first. It was controlled, precise. She would hold up the offending thing between two fingers, as if it were something spoiled.

“Do you think I’m your servant?”

That question followed us through childhood. It was waiting at the bottom of laundry baskets and inside unmade beds. It was folded into the smell of bleach and furniture polish. We did not think she was our servant, but we did not know how to answer. To say no sounded false. To say nothing made her fury rise.

She worked hard. Even as children we knew this. She rose before us, cooked for us, washed our clothes, remembered dentist appointments, ironed uniforms, found missing shoes, signed school forms, cut the crusts off sandwiches for the child who hated crusts and then shouted at that same child for being ungrateful. Her care was everywhere, undeniable and exhausting. It filled the cupboards, whitened the socks, kept the floors shining. It also pressed against us until we could hardly breathe.

Love in our house often arrived in the shape of accusation.

After she had shouted, she might make us breakfast. The toast would be buttered all the way to the edges. The tea would be poured just how we liked it. She would push a plate toward us, still breathing hard from anger, and tell us to eat before it got cold. If one of us cried, she became angrier, not because she did not care, but because our tears seemed to accuse her of something she could not bear to see.

“What are you crying for? I do everything for you.”

And she did. That was the trap of it. She did everything, and because she did everything, we owed her a gratitude so large it could never be paid. Every polished surface reflected back our failure. Every meal came with a debt. Every clean shirt carried the warning that we were loved, and that we were a burden.

My father, when he was there, made himself small. He hid behind the newspaper or left early for work, kissing the air near my mother’s cheek while she stood with her arms folded, already angry at the day. Sometimes he would wink at us as if to say, Let it pass. But it did not pass. It settled into the walls. It collected like dust in places even she could not reach.

We became experts in prevention. We wiped sinks dry after using them. We straightened cushions when we stood up. We carried our plates to the kitchen before being asked. We learned the particular silence of guilt, even when we had done nothing wrong. Our mornings were choreographed around her moods: one child feeding the dog, another clearing the table, another checking the hallway for shoes or toys that might set her off. We moved quickly, nervously, bumping into one another, whispering accusations.

“You left it there.”

“No, I didn’t.”

“Yes, you did. Move it before she sees.”

There were cobwebs in my memory, though she never allowed them to remain long in the house. I remember them in corners, silver and delicate, discovered with horror and destroyed with a broom. I remember the way she stretched to reach them, lips tight, as if each web had been spun deliberately to shame her. I remember clutter too: not much of it, because clutter was hunted down, but enough to cause panic. A pile of books. A jacket over a chair. Birthday cards left too long on the mantel. These ordinary things became dangerous in her presence. They were signs that the house was slipping out of control, and if the house slipped, perhaps everything else would too.

Only later did I wonder what she was truly fighting. Perhaps the dirt was easier to face than fear. Perhaps mess spoke to her of poverty, failure, judgment, the eyes of neighbors, the standards of her own mother, the life she had not meant to have. Perhaps cleaning was the one form of power available to her. With a cloth in her hand, she could restore order. She could make something shine. She could prove, at least for a moment, that she had not been defeated.

But as children, we did not know how to pity her without also fearing her. We only knew the heat of her temper, the shame that followed her inspections, the way she could turn a room cold with one look. We knew that she loved us fiercely and that her love could hurt. We knew that her hands, red from hot water and soap, had held us when we were ill, and those same hands had snatched toys away, slammed cupboards, pointed out our faults with devastating accuracy.

In that house, care and harm were not opposites. They were tangled together like threads in the same cloth. My mother’s devotion kept us fed, clothed, and safe from the outside world, but inside the home it made us watchful and afraid. She gave everything she had, then blamed us for the emptiness it left in her. We loved her, resented her, needed her, and escaped her in small ways whenever we could.

Morning after morning, the house gleamed. The windows shone. The floors were swept clean. No cobweb survived for long.

But beneath that brightness, something in us remained cluttered and unresolved: guilt, anger, loyalty, tenderness, and the old childhood instinct to look around quickly, find what was out of place, and fix it before my mother came into the room.
outputs.L5:
**For Mom**

For Mom, even the smallest mess never went unnoticed. A trail of mud by the door, a pile of dishes in the sink, or a corner gathering dust was not just filth to her—it was a sign that the home needed care.

She never cleaned with anger, though. She cleaned with patience, turning disorder into comfort. To her, a clean home was not about perfection; it was about love. Every swept floor and folded blanket was her quiet way of saying, “You are safe here.”

And even when life itself felt messy, Mom had a way of clearing the filth from our hearts too—with kindness, warmth, and a reminder that every day could begin again.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary memoir-style paragraph about growing up with a volatile, compulsively cleaning mother in a messy old house, using vivid sensory detail and a collective “we” voice.
counterfactuals.output: We grew up in a house that seemed always to be shedding itself—plaster dust sifting from the ceiling like old flour, paint curling from the windowsills, the hallways smelling of damp wood, boiled cabbage, and the sour rag left too long in the sink. Our mother moved through it with a bucket in one hand and a fury in the other, scrubbing as if the whole place had personally betrayed her. We learned the weather of her by sound: the slap of the mop against linoleum meant silence, the shriek of chair legs meant vanish, the cupboard doors banging open and shut meant some invisible stain had offended her and would soon become our fault. She cleaned compulsively, violently, polishing the cracked enamel stove until it shone in patches, bleaching the bathroom until our eyes watered, sweeping around the piles of newspapers, broken toys, and laundry that rose like small ruins in every room. We knew the sting of ammonia in the throat, the grit under bare feet, the cold dishwater where our wrists turned red. We knew how to stand very still while she raged at crumbs, at dust, at the muddy prints we had tracked in from the yard, though the roof leaked and mice nested in the walls and the old house breathed dirt back the moment she turned away. In that place, cleanliness was never calm; it was a storm we survived together, holding our breath in the bleach-bright air.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dark, lyrical first-person plural passage about siblings waking to their mother’s angry cleaning ritual, with themes of shame, family dysfunction, and childhood guilt.
counterfactuals.output:
We woke to the weather of her anger.

Not thunder, not shouting—not yet—but the hard, wet slap of the mop against the kitchen tiles, the bucket dragged like a body from room to room, the cupboards opened and shut with the judgment of doors in a courthouse. Before we knew the hour, we knew the crime: crumbs in the carpet, cups left breathing sour milk on the table, our socks like small dead animals under the couch. We lay in our beds pretending sleep had sealed us away, but guilt moved under our blankets with us, warm and wormlike.

She cleaned as if she could scour us out of her life and still keep us there.

The house filled with bleach and accusation. Its sharp white smell climbed the stairs, entered our mouths, stung the backs of our throats. We listened to her mutter our names into the sink, into the toilet bowl, into the black mouths of trash bags. Each syllable came back altered, less like a name than a debt. We were children, but already we understood that love could arrive wearing rubber gloves. That it could kneel, furious, beside a bathtub ring and call itself sacrifice.

We rose quietly, ashamed of our bodies, our hunger, our sleep. We made our beds too late. We gathered toys too late. We stood in doorways with our hands hanging uselessly at our sides, small defendants awaiting sentence. She did not look at us at first. That was worse. Her back, bent over the stove, said what her mouth did not: Look what you have done to me. Look what you have made of my life.

And we looked.

We looked at the red crescents in her palms where the brush had pressed. We looked at the hair fallen loose from her clip, the sweat at her temples, the terrible holiness of her rage. We wanted to save her from the mess and from us, from the father who slept through it, from the bills under the magnet, from the loneliness she polished into every surface until the whole house shone with it.

But we were the mess too.

We knew it in the way she stepped over us, in the way she sighed when we asked for breakfast, in the way our cereal bowls seemed to accuse us from the sink before we had even finished eating. Childhood was a room we kept failing to clean. We tracked ourselves everywhere. We left fingerprints on glass, breath on mirrors, need in the air.

By noon the house would be spotless and ruined. Sunlight would lie across the floors like forgiveness, but none of us believed it. We would move carefully through the gleaming rooms, afraid to touch what had been made pure by her suffering. She would sit at the table at last, silent, smelling of lemon and smoke, her face emptied of the storm that had passed through it.

We would love her then with the frightened devotion of prisoners. We would bring her drawings, apologies, cups of water she had not asked for. We would try to become good enough to quiet the bucket, the mop, the slammed drawers of morning.

But always, somewhere beneath the clean floor, our shame waited—damp, patient, shining—ready to rise with her before dawn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate prose in the style of a contemporary autobiographical essay: a mother with a hernia obsessively cleans cobwebs and berates her children while they scatter and react in different ways.
counterfactuals.output:
By ten in the morning my mother had already tied a dish towel around her waist like an apron and declared war on the ceiling.

The hernia sat beneath her blouse in a way that made all of us look away. It wasn’t dramatic, not in the way children expect illness to be dramatic—no blood, no collapse, no ambulance at the curb—but it changed the shape of her, and the shape of the house around her. She moved with one hand pressed against her abdomen, as if holding in a secret or keeping herself assembled. With the other hand she brandished the broom.

“Look at this,” she said, jabbing at a corner above the china cabinet. “Do you people not have eyes?”

We had eyes. We had too many eyes. We watched everything: the tremor in her wrist, the way her face tightened when she reached too high, the gray little banners of cobweb clinging to the plaster. We watched each other watching her.

My brother Marcus disappeared first. He had a talent for vanishing that bordered on spiritual. One moment he was at the kitchen table with a bowl of cereal, his spoon stopped halfway to his mouth, and the next he was gone, leaving the milk to film over in accusation. Later I would find him in the garage, sitting on an overturned bucket, taking apart a broken radio with the delicacy of a surgeon.

My sister Lena went the other direction: performance. She stood in the hallway with her arms crossed, thirteen and already fluent in contempt.

“You’re not supposed to be lifting things,” she said.

“I’m lifting dust,” my mother snapped. “Unless dust got heavy while I wasn’t looking.”

“You’re going to make it worse.”

“What’s worse is living like animals.”

The word animals moved through the house and found each of us. I felt it land on my shoulders, in my hair, under my fingernails. I was eleven, old enough to understand insult but young enough to believe it might be fact. I looked around at the shoes near the door, the school papers sliding from the counter, the couch cushions collapsed into soft craters. I saw suddenly what she saw: a family shedding evidence of itself everywhere.

My mother angled the broom upward again. The bristles scraped the ceiling with a dry, papery sound. A cobweb detached and floated down, graceful as ash. She flinched when it brushed her cheek.

“Get it,” she said to me.

I pinched it between two fingers. It was almost nothing, a little ghost of dirt.

“Throw it away. Don’t just stand there holding it.”

I carried it to the trash as if it were something alive.

There are mothers who keep their pain private, who retreat with it into bedrooms, who become quiet and remote as figures behind frosted glass. My mother externalized hers. Her body betrayed her, so the house had to answer. The baseboards, the curtains, the corners of rooms—everything became a witness for the prosecution. The cobwebs were not cobwebs. They were proof that we were ungrateful, careless, blind. Proof that she could not rest without the world taking advantage of her.

She had always cleaned, but after the hernia she cleaned as though chased. She wiped counters that were already clean. She refolded towels we had folded wrong. She opened closets and groaned at their contents like a woman discovering crimes. All the while she narrated our failures.

“Books on the floor. Cups in the bedrooms. Nobody rinses a plate. Nobody knows where the hamper is. I should put up a sign. Maybe then.”

My youngest brother, Peter, began to cry whenever she said “nobody,” because he thought she meant him specifically. He trailed her from room to room with a washcloth, desperate to be useful and always in the way.

“Not there,” she barked. “You’re smearing it.”

He froze, lower lip shining.

I hated her then with the clean, hot hatred available only to children, a hatred without context or mercy. I hated the broom, the towel, the bulge under her blouse. I hated the way she made the air in the house tense and granular, as if we were breathing dust. I hated that I pitied her, too. Pity felt like a chore she had assigned me without asking.

Lena finally snatched the broom from her hands.

“Stop,” she said.

The room went still.

My mother stared at her, not angry at first, but astonished. The house seemed to hold its breath around the two of them. Lena was almost as tall as she was by then, with the same dark hair, the same sharp chin. For one strange second they looked less like mother and daughter than two versions of the same woman meeting at the narrowest point of a life.

“Give it back,” my mother said.

“No.”

“You think you run this house?”

“I think you’re going to hurt yourself.”

My mother laughed once, a terrible little sound. “Now everybody’s concerned.”

But no one moved. Marcus had appeared in the doorway from wherever he’d been hiding, smelling faintly of oil and metal. Peter stood beside the sofa, clutching his washcloth in both hands. I hovered near the trash can, guilty and eager, waiting for someone else to decide what kind of family we were going to be.

Then my mother put both hands over the hernia. Her face changed. Not collapsed, exactly. Opened. The fury drained out so quickly it embarrassed all of us. Without it, she looked small and overworked, a woman in a house full of children who could outrun her pain but not understand it.

“Fine,” she said. “Live in filth.”

She went to her bedroom and shut the door with careful softness, which was worse than slamming it.

For a while we stayed where we were. Then Marcus took the broom from Lena and began, awkwardly, to sweep the ceiling corners. Lena picked up the shoes by the door, muttering that everybody in this family was insane. Peter wiped the coffee table in solemn circles. I climbed onto a chair and reached for the cobweb above the window, the one my mother had not gotten to yet.

It came away easily. That surprised me. How fragile the thing was, after all that. How little force it took to clear a corner, and how much to live inside a body that had turned against you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an emotionally intense scene from childhood about a harsh but loving mother, spiders, clutter, siblings, and the narrator’s conflicted feelings of fear, guilt, and attachment.
counterfactuals.output:
When I was small, the house was never quiet enough for fear to hide properly.

It had to crouch among things.

It lived in the leaning towers of mail on the kitchen counter, in the laundry baskets that had become permanent furniture, in the cereal boxes left open on top of the refrigerator, their waxy mouths gaping. It lived in the hallway where shoes piled like shed skins, where my brothers’ plastic dinosaurs and my sister’s hair clips waited in ambush underfoot. It lived behind the curtains that never quite closed and beneath the couch cushions where crumbs, pennies, and lost crayons made a country of their own.

And in the corners, always, there were spiders.

My mother saw them before anyone else did. She could be stirring powdered milk into macaroni, yelling at my oldest brother to stop kicking the table, telling my sister not to wipe her nose on her sleeve, and suddenly her eyes would snap to the ceiling.

“Don’t move,” she’d say.

We all froze.

There, where the wall met the yellowing ceiling, a spider would cling in its quiet, terrible patience.

My mother hated spiders with a fury that seemed larger than the spiders themselves. She hated them like they had insulted her, like they had crept in on purpose to humiliate her in front of her children. Her face would tighten, and she’d snatch a shoe from the floor or a rolled-up magazine from the stack on the counter.

“Get back,” she’d say, though none of us were moving. “I said get back.”

Her voice could slice the room open.

I was afraid of spiders, but I was more afraid of her fear. It transformed her. My mother, who could carry two bags of groceries on each arm and a sleeping child against her hip, who could scrub a pot until it shone, who could braid my sister’s hair so tight it made her eyes water, would become wild at the sight of one small black shape.

She climbed chairs that wobbled under her. She swung hard. Sometimes she missed, and the spider dropped.

That was the worst part.

The falling.

We screamed then — all of us — scattering into one another, knocking into the clutter, tripping over toys, our terror multiplying in the cramped room. My little brother would cry without knowing why. My sister would cover her mouth with both hands. I would feel my whole body go cold and ashamed, because some part of me wanted my mother to kill it, and another part of me could not bear the sound it made when she did.

A small crunch.

A smear.

“See?” she’d say, breathing hard, wiping the shoe on a paper towel. “It’s gone. You’re safe.”

But she didn’t sound relieved. She sounded angry at us for needing safety, angry at the house for giving her enemies, angry at herself for being afraid.

Then, almost always, she would turn on us.

“Why is this place such a mess?” she’d shout, as if the spider had been born from our socks and plates and school papers. “Do you think I can do everything? Do you think I’m your maid?”

No one answered. We knew better.

Her love was like that: a blanket yanked up to your chin so hard it stole your breath.

She would slap the counter with her palm, point at the dishes, the floor, the overflowing trash. My older brother would mutter something, and she’d whirl on him. My sister would start crying, and my mother would say, “Don’t you start,” though her own eyes were shining. I would bend down and gather whatever was closest — blocks, a spoon, a sock stiff with old mud — desperate to become useful, to make myself small and good.

I hated her then.

I loved her so much I thought it would split me open.

Because after the shouting, after the spider was dead and the room had been punished for containing it, she would find me somewhere — under the table, beside the washing machine, in the narrow space between the couch and the wall where I liked to wedge myself when the house felt too full.

She never apologized in words.

Instead she would stand there for a moment, large and tired, smelling of dish soap and sweat and the onion she had chopped for dinner. Then she’d say, “Come here.”

I never knew if it was a command or a rescue.

I always went.

Her arms were strong. Too strong, sometimes. She held me like she was trying to keep the whole world from prying me loose, like love was a grip and not a gift. My cheek pressed against her stomach, soft through her old T-shirt. I could hear the churn and growl of her body, the life in her. Her hand moved over my hair, rough at first, then gentler.

“You know I don’t like yelling,” she’d say.

I knew she didn’t like spiders either, but she still crushed them.

“I just need help,” she’d murmur. “I can’t do it all alone.”

And there it was — the heavy thing she placed in my arms without meaning to. Her loneliness. Her exhaustion. Her fear. I held it because I loved her. I held it because I was a child and thought love meant proving you were not a burden.

From the kitchen my brothers would begin fighting again. My sister would call for someone to find her shoe. The sink would still be full. The dead spider would still be folded inside the paper towel at the top of the trash, not gone at all, only hidden.

My mother would let me go and wipe her face with the heel of her hand.

“Alright,” she’d say, voice hardening back into shape. “Enough. Everybody clean.”

And we would.

We would move through that crowded, breathing house, lifting piles, closing drawers, sweeping crumbs into our palms. All the while I watched the corners. I watched for the next dark twitch of legs, the next tiny trespass that would summon my mother’s rage and courage together.

I was afraid of the spiders because they came from nowhere.

I was afraid of my mother because she came from everywhere.

But at night, when the house finally sagged into silence and my siblings slept in tangled blankets around me, I would listen for her footsteps. I would wait for the hallway floorboards to complain under her weight, for the pause outside our door.

Sometimes she came in.

She would think we were asleep. She would step over the clutter with the careful grace of someone crossing a minefield. In the dim light, she looked smaller. Not weak, exactly, but used up. She would tuck the blanket around my little brother, move a stuffed animal from under my sister’s neck, brush my hair from my face with fingers that had scrubbed and struck and soothed.

If she saw a spider then, she killed it quietly.

No shouting. No sermon. Just a quick press of tissue to wall, a whispered curse, a glance toward us to make sure we hadn’t woken.

Once, I opened my eyes and saw her standing over my bed, holding a crushed tissue in her fist.

She looked caught. Guilty, almost.

“Go back to sleep,” she whispered.

I wanted to ask her if she was scared. I wanted to tell her I was sorry for the mess, for the noise, for every spider that had ever entered our house. I wanted to tell her not to be angry. I wanted to tell her to climb into the bed with us and let somebody else stand guard.

Instead I closed my eyes.

A moment later, I felt her lips touch my forehead — dry, quick, fierce.

Then she was gone, leaving behind the faint smell of soap, the creak of the floor, and the terrible comfort of knowing that if something frightened us in the dark, she would come with a shoe in her hand, furious and trembling, ready to save us from what she could not bear.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a polished literary nonfiction excerpt describing a chaotic household morning where the mother attacks dirt and disorder, the children evade her anger, and the narration ends with “We must have deserved it.”
counterfactuals.output:
By seven, the house had begun its daily surrender.

Cereal hardened in bowls. Socks appeared in doorways like small, defeated animals. A ribbon of toothpaste clung to the bathroom sink, bright as evidence. In the kitchen, the linoleum shone in patches where our mother had already attacked it, rag in one hand, broom in the other, her face tightened by the private arithmetic of labor: what had been done, what had been ruined, what would have to be done again.

She moved from room to room with a terrible purpose, flinging open curtains, snapping sheets, slapping dust from the backs of chairs. Dirt was not a condition in our house; it was an insult. Disorder was not the natural weather of children; it was betrayal. She pursued crumbs beneath the table as if they had hidden from her on purpose. She scrubbed at fingerprints on the refrigerator door until the metal squealed. When she found our shoes in the hall, our books on the floor, our damp towels breathing mildew into the corners, she called our names with a force that made each syllable feel like a charge being read aloud.

We learned to scatter. One of us vanished behind the sofa with a spelling list. One slipped into the yard without a coat. Another took refuge in the bathroom and sat fully dressed on the edge of the tub, feet lifted from the floor as though the tiles themselves might report us. We communicated by glances, by the creak of stairs, by the altered pitch of her voice. We knew which cabinets could be opened quietly, which floorboards betrayed weight, which apologies would soften her and which would sharpen her further.

Still, she found us. She always found us—not because she was cruel, but because she was everywhere: in the smell of bleach, in the wet shine of the counters, in the frantic holiness of a house being made clean before anyone could live in it. Her anger filled the rooms the way morning light did, touching everything, exposing everything.

And we, guilty in ways we could not name, stood before her with our hair uncombed, our mouths sugared, our hands empty.

We must have deserved it.
